content: Wrap rage, also known as wrapping rage or package rage, refers to intense feelings of anger, frustration, and even violent behavior that arise when individuals struggle to open packaging that is particularly difficult to remove. This phenomenon gained official recognition in 2006 when Consumer Reports magazine introduced the Oyster Awards, which highlighted products with the most challenging packaging to open. An example of wrap rage was humorously depicted on The Colbert Report, where host Stephen Colbert attempted, unsuccessfully, to use a knife to open the packaging of a new calculator. This struggle exemplifies the frustration many people experience with such packaging. When individuals attempt to open these packages while experiencing wrap rage, they often use tools or implements in a hasty and unsafe manner, applying excessive force. This reckless approach can lead to minor injuries, such as cuts, bruises, or sprains to the fingers and hands. In some cases, it may even cause muscle strains, such as in the shoulder, due to the physical exertion required to open the packaging. Beyond personal injuries, wrap rage can also result in damage to the product itself. For instance, instruction manuals, CDs, or warranty cards enclosed within the packaging may be torn or otherwise damaged during the opening process. Additionally, nearby items may be inadvertently harmed during these attempts. Another issue associated with wrap rage is the impact on product returns. Certain types of packaging, such as blister packs, often require significant force to open, which can render the packaging irreparably damaged. Many stores have policies that require returned goods to be in their original packaging, making it impossible to return items once the packaging has been forcibly opened.
